results.message: Why can't I stop thinking about things I don't want to think about?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
You are asking a question we spent our whole lives learning to answer. We had a name for what you are describing: the logismoi - the unwanted, intruding thoughts that come at you without being invited. We treated them as the main battlefield of this life, once the empire stopped killing Christians and the fight moved inward. You cannot stop them by will alone - that much we knew from long experience. What we learned instead was to watch them as they came, catch them early while they were still small, and answer them on the spot rather than let them settle in and grow.

One of us, Evagrius, made a whole system of it - he named eight kinds of thoughts that attack in patterns, gave each one its own character, and taught a method he called antirrhesis: you talk back to the thought with a fitting line of Scripture the moment it arrives. He wrote it down as a handbook, matching thought to verse, so a person would have the weapon ready when the attack came. He also named the goal all that discipline served: apatheia - not apathy, but freedom from the passions that drive a person, won slowly through the long work of stilling what pulls you. And he was honest about what lies underneath: "Mere abstention from evil things is not perfection - only if thou hast entered into thy ruined mind, and hast slain the serpent that lies under the mind beneath the surface of the thoughts, and burrows into what we call the secret chambers and storehouses of the soul and murders thee - for the heart is a deep gulf".

We should tell you plainly: Evagrius was unusually educated for one of us, trained in Greek philosophy in a way most of our people were not, and his system is his own construction more than it is the wider movement's shared vocabulary. But the struggle he was naming was ours, not his invention. The thoughts come to everyone. What he gave us was one way to name them rightly and fight them deliberately, rather than be pulled around by them without knowing what was happening.

The other thing we can tell you - and this one goes deeper than any system - is that the struggle is not yours to win by your own strength alone. We argued this one out at length when it was put to us directly: if a man strives with all his might, can he become master of what is good by effort alone? The answer we gave was no, not unless he has it as a gift. We held that grace and free will look opposed to each other but really are in harmony. One of us put it this way: "...now He puts into us the very beginnings of salvation, and gives to each the zeal of his free will; and now grants the carrying out of the work, and the perfecting of goodness; and now saves men, even against their will and without their knowledge, from ruin that is close at hand, and a headlong fall". Sometimes God puts the beginning into you; sometimes he carries the work through; sometimes he saves you from a fall you did not even see coming. It is not all on you to force.

The tradition also tells it this way, in the one story we kept that shows the whole fight from beginning to breakthrough: Antony shut himself inside an abandoned tomb to face the logismoi at their worst. Demons came at him in a crowd and beat him until he could not speak. When they came again, now in the shapes of wild beasts, he answered them in words we still keep: "If there had been any power in you, it would have sufficed had one of you come, but since the Lord hath made you weak, you attempt to terrify me by numbers: and a proof of your weakness is that you take the shapes of brute beasts". At the worst of it, a light broke into the tomb and the pain left him. He asked where the light had been at the start of his struggle, and was told it had been there

sources.author: Pseudo-Macarius - the attribution the Internet Archive itself uses for this very item ('by Pseudo-Macarius; Macarius, the Egyptian, Saint, 4th cent; Mason, Arthur James, 1851-1928'), leading with the ascription Mason spent his Introduction arguing against. Ascribed traditionally to Macarius the Egyptian (c. 300-391 CE), the Scetis elder; that ascription rests on the manuscripts alone, and the Bodleian manuscript titles the collection an epistle 'to the Abbot Symeon of Mesopotamia of Syria'. Modern scholarship generally treats the corpus as pseudonymous - a Syrian or Mesopotamian author of the late fourth or early fifth century, with a disputed relation to the condemned Messalian current.
sources.work: Fifty Spiritual Homilies - a connected body of ascetic teaching on the interior life: the indwelling of the Spirit, grace as something experienced rather than inferred, the coexistence of sin and grace in the baptised, the soul as the bride of Christ, and the long combat that continues after grace is received. The affective and experiential counterpart to the intellectualist psychology this world already holds from Evagrius and Cassian.

results.message: Is God something a person can actually experience, or do you just decide to believe?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We had one current among us that said yes - God can be known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. "Only let a man strive to be a friend of His and well pleasing to Him, and in real experience and feeling he shall truly see the good things of heaven, and the inexpressible delights and infinite riches of Godhead". The same voice taught it this way: "For the soul that is privileged to be in communion with the Spirit of His light, and is irradiated by the beauty of the unspeakable glory of Him who has prepared her to be a seat and a dwelling for Himself, becomes all light, all face, all eye; and there is no part of her that is not full of the spiritual eyes of light". This was not the only way we spoke of knowing God - another current, more systematic, had the mind clear itself until it beheld its own proper radiance - but this one held plainly that the experience is real, not imagined or merely hoped for.

We should tell you honestly: this voice is one current within our tradition, not the whole of it, and we will not flatten the difference between them. Most of us did not argue about God for a living; we were formed to see him. The deepest of us - and only a few went this deep - held that God is known less by argument than by a long stilling of the passions that otherwise crowd the mind: strip away what drives you, and in the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before.

But our own words are not confession. The sayings we kept were meant to redirect a struggling person, not to confess a doubt. We show you a struggle disciplined. We do not show you a doubt confessed. If you are asking what to do when you cannot believe - how to navigate the gap between deciding and experiencing - that question is not answered in our own words the way you are asking it. What we can tell you is that some among us held the experience to be real, earned through the long work of becoming the kind of person who can receive it, not forced by an act of will. The striving and the receiving were held together, not set against each other.

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We did not disagree about whether a woman could be an elder - amma, the honored address for a proven woman elder, is our own word, used the same way abba was used for a man. What we cannot tell you is how common it was, or whether anyone among us held that it should not have been allowed at all. The sayings we kept from women elders survive, and they were kept the same way we kept any elder's sayings - short words given for one moment of need, carrying teaching weight. We have Sarah's own words, still kept among us: "It is I who am a man, and ye who are women" - said to elder monks who had come to test her on the ground of her sex. Those words were preserved and passed down. That tells you they mattered enough to someone to write down and keep.

But we should tell you plainly what is missing. The women in our record arrive late - in one collection, thirty-four chapters of men first, then the women announced in their own section, as though the author had to justify including them before he wrote about them. And we do not have a woman speaking at length in her own person the way we have from some of the men - no first-person account by a woman survives in this material, though the men of that same book are also narrated in third person rather than speaking for themselves, so the asymmetry is not that simple. What that means is we cannot tell you whether the silence is because fewer women held that kind of authority, or because later hands who gathered the sayings into collections chose to keep fewer of them, or both.

The other thing we cannot give you is a scene showing anyone among us arguing about it directly - whether a woman should or should not carry an elder's authority is a question the tension itself suggests, but no story we kept dramatizes anyone actually fighting over it. We lived with more than one unresolved tension. This may have been one of them. What we will not do is invent an agreement or a controversy our own record does not show.
